newsitem.title: USA: UPS settlement may raise wage pressures-analysts.
newsitem.headline: UPS settlement may raise wage pressures-analysts.

text.p: The sweeping concessions that workers won to end a 15-day strike against United Parcel Service may put upward pressure on wages but were unlikely to increase inflation, economists said on Tuesday.

"It will contribute to the perception of wage pressure," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at the brokerage A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc. "But at this point, it doesn't look that inflationary for the economy. It's too early to assume this is a problem."

UPS, the world's largest package delivery company, settled with the Teamsters union late on Monday after a 15-day strike. The walkout by 185,000 workers, the biggest in 21 years, cost UPS about $650 million and crippled many businesses.

The union won on several key issues. Under the agreement, the company will convert 10,000 part-time jobs into full-time jobs over five years and hourly wage rates will rise as much as 36 percent over the same period.
Teamsters President Ron Carey said the tentative agreement was a major victory for organized labor. "Working people were on the run, but not anymore," Carey declared. "This strike marks a new era."
Wall Street analysts said labor's victory could have economic implications beyond UPS and the 185,000 workers.
"This was a watershed event," said David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co. Inc.

"Clearly the union had a major victory. Now other workers, whether union or non-union, will act on this highly publicized settlement in this tight labor market to demand increases in their wages and benefits," he added.
But other economists were not as sure that the effects of the settlement would spill over into the economy.
William Dickens, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington, said UPS was willing to make concessions other employers would shun.

"I don't think there's any bad news in it for inflation prospects," he said. "UPS is a very unusual employer. It wants to have a cordial relationship with its union and its employees. That's not typical of U.S. employers. Most will fight like junkyard dogs with unions."
National Association of Manufacturers economist Gordon Richards told Reuters Financial Television that fears of wage pressure and increased inflation were unfounded.
"In my mind, some of the fears of wage pressure are unnecessarily alarmist," Richards said. "We're still looking at a decelerating or at least stable inflation rate."
One thing that is clear is that the Federal Reserve had been keeping a close eye on the strike. Last week, the central bank asked UPS to describe the walkout's economic impact.
"This is an event the Fed has been watching for," said John Challenger, executive vice president of Chicago-based consulting firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas Inc.

"It's not going to affect this (Fed) meeting," he said. "But (Fed policy-makers) are going to be scrutinizing labor data in the coming months to see if there are other signs that wage pressure has passed a certain place along the road."
The Fed on Tuesday left key interest rates unchanged amid evidence the economy is growing at a comfortable speed with low inflation.
